transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-10-05 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Jordan Myers (Nimbus CTO), Leah Ortiz (Nimbus ML Eng), Sam Holden (Nimbus SRE), Maya Singh (Product)

Summary:
Quick kickoff for migration from current multi-vendor endpoints (OpenAI + Anthropic + Together) into Redwood API. Focus: parity mapping, console/Optimize walkthrough, baseline perf expectations, VPC/on-prem constraints and security checklist. Agreement to run pilot benchmarks and share prompt families.

Topics covered:
- Parity mapping (model name mappings, function-calls, streaming semantics)
- Console tour: routing, rollouts, metrics, traces
- Redwood Optimize recommendations: batching, KV/prefix cache, quantization suggestions
- Security: SOC2, KMS/HSM, VPC peering, audit logs and retention
- Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs: cost, SLOs, fallback policies

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we, uh, really appreciate you carving out time. Quick round of intros?
[00:10] Jordan (Nimbus): Jordan here, CTO. Leah is our ML lead, Sam is our infra lead, Maya on product. We're primarily evaluating latency and output parity, and want a clear migration path without two months of rework.
[00:20] Alex: Great. Samira, Diego — quick hi?
[00:22] Samira (Redwood SE): Hi all — Samira here, I'll be the technical lead on the demo and bench runs. We'll cover API parity and some examples of mapping prompts and function calling.
[00:30] Diego (Redwood): Diego — solutions eng, here to talk metrics and console flows.
[00:35] Leah (Nimbus): Quick note — we use both OpenAI function-calling for structured output and Anthropic chat completions for some safety mode stuff. Also Together for a subset of internal models. So a fair bit of heterogeneity.
[00:47] Alex: That's perfect context. The goal of today is to show how Redwood maps those semantics, where we can hit parity, and where customers typically accept small output differences in exchange for latency/cost wins.
[00:58] Jordan: Sounds good. Also, we'll probably ask about tokens per month and burst capacity — our user flows have weekly spikes.
[01:05] Samira: Absolutely. We'll show Dedicated/reserved capacity and autoscaling options, and fallback routing.

[01:22] Samira: Ok I'm sharing my screen — the Redwood Console. Top left is model catalog — you'll see both Redwood-verified model profiles and open variants. For example, we have a mapped profile for 'gpt-like-xxl' that we typically recommend mapping from OpenAI's gpt-4-ish endpoints. Note that naming is opinionated here to avoid vendor names in customer infra.
[01:45] Leah: Are model parameters locked? Like temperature, top-p?
[01:50] Samira: You can set defaults at route-level and override per request. We also expose a rollout layer so you can pin a percentage of traffic to a new model variant.
[02:05] Diego: On the right you can see the routing policies — latency-first, cost-first, region-restricted; you can attach fallbacks so if your primary model is at capacity we route to a cheaper variant automatically.
[02:20] Sam Holden: That fallback story is big for us. Our error budget is tight during spikes. Do you do automatic KV cache reuse across routed models?
[02:32] Samira: Good question. KV/prefix cache is scope-bound — we can share caches between a small family of compatible quantized variants, but not across wildly different architectures. There is an optimization step in the platform that suggests which variants are cache-compatible.

[02:55] Jordan: Talk to us about function-calling equivalence. Our product uses structured outputs extensively. We've had shape drift when we moved between vendors previously.
[03:10] Samira: Right — we have a parity mapping doc that maps function signatures and expected JSON shapes. Redwood's API supports the function-calling pattern (name+schema) and will return a structured object similar to OpenAI. A few caveats: tokenization differences can change whitespace and punctuation, and safety filters can modify output. We log both original model output and the post-processed parse so you can compare.
[03:35] Leah: Do you preserve turn-level metadata? We rely on assistant messages to contain tooling metadata and sources.
[03:42] Samira: Yes, we preserve message-level metadata, but some provider-specific fields will be normalized. We'll include the original provider tag in the trace so you can diff.

[04:00] Diego: Now, switching to Optimize — this is our recommendations panel. Based on a sample trace you upload we suggest batch sizes, KV cache TTLs, and quantization target for throughput vs quality. For example, for chat-like short-turn workloads we often recommend 4–8 token batch/window with small prefix caches. For longer-context summarization we favor larger KV cache retention and aggressive batching.
[04:27] Maya (Nimbus): Does Optimize auto-apply rules or is it advisory?
[04:32] Diego: Advisory by default, but org admins can enable auto-apply on non-prod routes. We also have a dry-run mode to estimate cost impact before applying.

[04:45] Jordan: On encryption — we need customer-managed keys for audit regs. KMS/HSM?
[04:50] Alex: We support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and can enable customer-managed keys for both data at-rest and some transit-level keys. For Private deployments you can plug in an HSM. We also produce audit logs in S3 with retention controls.
[05:05] Sam Holden: Network — can we do VPC peering / private endpoints? We run in a locked-down subnet with strict egress rules.
[05:12] Samira: Yes — Redwood Private supports VPC peering and private link endpoints. We'll need your network diagram; Diego will link our VPC requirements doc. Some customers run the control plane in Redwood but keep inference nodes in their VPCs.

[05:35] Jordan: Costs — show us an example of token pricing vs dedicated reserved GPU. We want a sanity check.
[05:42] Alex: I'll drop a simple excel after the call — we price hosted per-token and dedicated as reserved instance plus utilization. For heavy steady-state workloads reserved is typically cheaper. There's a quick calc in Optimize that uses your throughput profile to recommend reserved capacity sizes.

[06:00] [Small crosstalk]
[06:15] Leah: Quick nit — when you say streaming parity, does Redwood stream chunked deltas in the same shape that OpenAI streaming does? We have a frontend that reassembles delta chunks.
[06:28] Samira: We emulate streaming semantics; minor differences in boundary tokenization can occur. We provide an SDK shim that normalizes chunk headers to match common client expectations.

[06:45] Jordan: Okay, let's walk through a concrete migration example — we have an endpoint that does multi-step Q/A with a tool plugin for database lookups and function calling. We need output determinism for our acceptance tests.
[07:00] Samira: Great — if you can share the prompt families and the current golden outputs, we can run a parity bench. Typical process is: you give 100–200 representative prompts, we run them across the mapped Redwood models and your current vendors, capture tokenization diffs, and produce a drift report with suggestions.
[07:25] Leah: How do you measure drift? Just BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics?
[07:30] Diego: We use a combination: structural JSON diff for function calls, semantic similarity metrics for free text, plus human-eval sampling for business-critical prompts. We flag changes that alter intent or remove entities.

[07:50] Maya: For acceptance, we need a rollback plan. If we push a route to 100% and see a spike in error or user complaints, what's the process?
[07:58] Alex: Rollouts are incremental by default; canaries, A/B. You can set automatic rollback triggers — e.g., if latency p50 or error rate crosses threshold we rollback or divert to a fallback vendor.

[08:20] Jordan: About model naming again — you mentioned avoiding vendor names. Will that break any of our current telemetry dashboards that assume provider labels in the header?
[08:30] Diego: We include a mapping layer and an export that attaches both the Redwood canonical name and the upstream provider name. So your telemetry can either consume canonical names or the original provider string.

[08:48] [Pause — 8:50–09:10 screen load noise]
[09:12] Samira: Ok, demo time — I'm going to show a sample parity mapping sheet. Column A: vendor endpoint, Column B: Redwood route, Column C: function-call JSON mapping notes, Column D: expected token delta.
[09:30] Leah: Token delta? In practice that's been the worst surprise as punctuation changes stuff.
[09:36] Samira: Yep. We estimate token delta based on tokenizer simulation. For example, a particular Anthropic style system message might add 12 tokens relative to GPT tokenization in practice. We include a delta so you can understand cost variance.

[09:55] Jordan: Do you support custom system messages or pre-prompts at route level?
[09:58] Samira: You can set a route pre-prompt and also attach middleware that injects user-specific context. This is where KV/prefix cache saves tokens — we cache prefix context where valid.

[10:20] Sam Holden: For SRE, what's the SLA on Dedicated nodes? We need numbers for internal docs.
[10:27] Alex: Dedicated comes with an SLA for uptime and latency SLOs (we'll send the exact SLA doc). Typical committed throughput examples are in the dedicated spec but we'll align on a throughput target for the pilot and include latency p50/p95 targets.

[10:45] Samira: Now switching to security — we have an SSO integration sample; Redwood supports SAML/SCIM provisioning and RBAC by route. Audit logs include request/response hashes and who changed configuration. Some fields are redacted in logs by default to meet PII policies, but we can change retention windows per contract.

[11:10] Leah: We require SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 evidence.
[11:14] Alex: We have SOC2 Type II and ISO certs — I'll attach certs to the doc share. For Private we also support additional compliance add-ons.

[11:30] Diego: Back to Optimize — here's an example recommendation for your chat workload. For 80% short-turn messages we recommend a medium-sized Ada-quantized variant with aggressive prefix caching. That approach reduced token cost in a past customer by ~38% while preserving top-level metrics.
[11:55] Jordan: What's the risk to answer quality with quantization?
[12:00] Samira: Depends on model size and temperature. For closed-domain retrieval-augmented tasks quantization often has minimal impact; for creative generation we caution heavier quantization. Optimize gives a quality delta estimate.

[12:20] Maya: About observability, can we get token-level breakdown by route and user? We need per-feature cost allocation for billing.
[12:28] Diego: Yes — cost attribution exists down to token per-route per-token-type. There's an exported CSV and a dashboard. You can map to internal teams or features via metadata tags in each request.

[12:48] Jordan: Okay can we go deeper on an example: this is a sample prompt that calls our DB tool and then emits JSON.
[13:00] Samira: (reads sample) Alright, on a function-call we'll show both the model's raw text and the parsed call. Here you'll see where we normalize key names — the raw call has 'userId' but we normalize to 'user_id' per your schema if you enable mapping.

[13:30] Leah: Does Redwood do any semantic post-processing? We prefer it to be a pure pipe but sometimes we want light post-processing to guarantee schema.
[13:38] Samira: We offer optional post-processing steps you can opt into — schema enforcement and whitespace trimming. They run as part of the route pipeline and are configurable.

[13:55] Jordan: How does billing show when you run fallbacks? If we route to cheaper variant is cost savings visible per-request?
[14:03] Diego: Yes — each request logs the model used and token counts; Optimize reconciles actual spend per route. If a fallback kicks in you still see both the attempted and the executed model in the logs.

[14:20] [Clip of typing]
[14:30] Samira: Next — pilot plan suggestion. We'll do a 2-week pilot: week 1 is parity testing on 500 prompts, week 2 we run an extended bench at scale (simulated spikes) and test rollouts. We'll measure latency p50/p95, error rates, token delta and semantic drift.
[14:52] Jordan: Do you sim traffic patterns? Our peaks are short-lived but intense; we don't want to overprovision.
[15:00] Samira: We simulate traffic bursts and can apply autoscaling policies with burst buffers. There's a burst-capacity option for Dedicated customers too.

[15:15] Sam Holden: For the bench we need guidance on what regions to test. We have users across NA and EU.
[15:22] Diego: We'll test both us-east and eu-west to match your production. We'll also run synthetic tests with half and full context windows to show perf curves.

[15:40] Maya: Can we review a sample audit log CSV?
[15:44] Alex: I'll attach an example. Logs include request id, route, model, token in/out, timestamp, user metadata (if provided), and a hash of the response to support replay-safe audits.

[16:00] [Small pause]
[16:08] Leah: One last tricky bit — we have a legacy fallback to Together for a particular internal model. Together uses a different tokeniser; will that be an edge case?
[16:18] Samira: We'll include tokenizer emulator in the parity run. Where tokenization introduces drift we add post-processing or small prompt-engineering changes to minimize user-visible differences. Sometimes the fix is to standardize a system preamble.

[16:35] Jordan: Timebox: what's the minimal set to get a pilot running?
[16:40] Alex: Minimum: 1) Share 200 prompts + golden outputs, 2) provide network diagram and egress constraints, 3) grant a read-only sample of telemetry or export. After that we can run a 3–5 day preliminary parity report.

[17:00] [Filler, laughter]
[17:12] Samira: Alright I'm going to quickly show a parity report example — here you can see line items: prompt id, provider outputs, token delta, semantic score, recommended remediation (prompt tweak, model variant, or post-processing). There are severity levels for anything that changes semantic intent.
[17:37] Leah: For remediations that require prompt changes, do you version those recommendations so we can audit when we altered prompts?
[17:43] Diego: Yes — every recommended change is a Git-style patch with author and timestamp in the console.

[18:00] Jordan: Good. Also, our legal team will want controls: retention schedules, who can see logs, and DPA language.
[18:10] Alex: We'll share the DPA and standard contract clauses. For retention we can set custom periods; some fields can be redacted on ingest to meet your needs.

[18:30] Maya: Any gotchas around streaming and websockets? Our frontend expects chunked delta tokens and the earlier vendor had slightly different chunk formats causing reconnection logic to break.
[18:42] Samira: We provide an SDK that normalizes deltas and reconnect semantics. It's a small client shim. Diego: we also expose a raw streaming endpoint if you want to manage reassembly yourself.

[19:00] Jordan: Ok, last few questions — if we want to keep inference in our VPC but use Redwood control plane, what are the latency implications?
[19:10] Diego: If inference nodes are in your VPC, network hop is minimized — you should see lower egress costs too. The control plane calls are mostly orchestration and are low-frequency. We can provide a POC deployment diagram for that.

[19:30] Sam Holden: For the POC, can you run a 10k user synthetic on our workload pattern?
[19:36] Samira: Yep, that's part of the pilot. We'll coordinate capacity needs — likely a mix of Dedicated reserved capacity and short-term burst.

[19:50] Jordan: Anything we should be aware of in terms of model weight differences causing hallucination rate changes?
[19:58] Samira: Hallucination changes can occur. Our approach is to monitor hallucination-rate proxies — wrong-entity extraction, contradictory statements vs provided context — and tie eval prompts to quality alerts so rollouts can be gated.

[20:20] Leah: Can we integrate our existing eval harness with Redwood's eval hooks?
[20:26] Diego: Yes — we have a webhook-based eval integration and an S3 import for large eval collections.

[20:40] [Longer demo pause 20:40–22:00 while screen is shared]
[22:05] Maya: Very helpful. What's your usual time-to-pilot?
[22:10] Alex: From signature to pilot usually 2–4 weeks; for Private/Onprem it can be longer due to network and procurement timelines. For a hosted pilot we can typically start in under a week.

[22:28] Jordan: Procurement will want cost scenarios. Can you include a few conservative/worst-case scenarios in the spreadsheet?
[22:34] Alex: Yes, I'll include low/med/high usage models and both hosted and dedicated cost projections.

[22:50] Samira: Quick callouts on common mapping issues we see: 1) function-call schema drift, 2) tokenizer-induced token deltas, 3) safety-filter variance. We generally handle 1&2 via mappings and small prompt deltas; 3 requires policy tuning.

[23:12] Leah: That safety-filter variance — do you allow customers to opt-out of Redwood's safety layer and rely solely on upstream model safety?
[23:20] Alex: For enterprise customers we can configure safety filter levels. For regulated sectors we often recommend additional filtering in your pipeline.

[23:35] Jordan: Alright, time check — we have 35 minutes left, do you want to run a short live demo or keep this high-level?
[23:42] Samira: Let's do a quick live parity run on one exemplar prompt. I'll paste a sample from Leah.

[24:00] Leah: Paste coming now — it's a multi-turn product spec question that uses a DB lookup.
[24:10] Samira: Running... (sound of keyboard) — results in. First, here's the OpenAI output, here's Anthropic, here's Together, and here's Redwood mapped output.
[24:30] Samira: You can see small formatting diffs in arrays, but the parsed function-call is structurally equivalent. Token delta: +6 vs OpenAI on this prompt due to tokenizer differences. Semantic score: 0.98.
[24:45] Jordan: Looks promising. Can you save the comparison?
[24:48] Samira: Saved and I'll include in the parity report.

[25:00] Diego: I'll also attach the trace with timing: p50 220ms, p95 480ms on this small test in us-east for the Redwood variant.

[25:20] Sam Holden: Those numbers are good. We'll want more large-scale bench numbers before committing.

[25:35] Maya: For the pilot, who's the day-to-day Redwood contact?
[25:40] Alex: I'll be the AE for commercial items; Samira is your SE for day-to-day technical work; Diego will support on metrics.

[25:50] Jordan: Any legal caveats for data residency? We have EU-only data for a product line.
[25:58] Alex: We can ensure region isolation — hosted EU regions, or Private deployment in your VPC for full locality. 

[26:12] Leah: For runbooks — do you provide a migration playbook? We want a checklist.
[26:18] Samira: Yes — we have a migration playbook: inventory endpoints -> map function-calls -> run 200-sample parity -> apply minor prompt changes -> pilot run -> roll to canary -> full roll. We'll share that doc.

[26:40] Jordan: Great — last question: in the case of a sudden model regression, what's your suggested emergency flow?
[26:48] Alex: Immediate steps: enable fallback route to previous variant, create an incident in your tracker, run a slice of failed prompts through the parity harness to see regression delta, then revert rollouts. We can also push a hotfix route to route traffic to a safe vendor until fixes are applied.

[27:10] [Silence while people nod]
[27:25] Samira: Ok final recap and next steps: 1) Alex sends parity mapping sheet + cost model (due 2026-10-08), 2) Nimbus shares 200 prompts + network diagram (due 2026-10-09), 3) Samira provisions trial keys and runs initial 500-parity tests (report due 2026-10-12), 4) Schedule a 60-min bench on 2026-10-13.

[27:52] Jordan: That timeline works. Any obvious blockers? Procurement will ask for SOC2 and DPA — we expect those.
[28:00] Alex: We'll include certs and DPA. Also I'll log action items in the CRM and send calendar invites for the pilot bench.

[28:10] Maya: Thanks everyone — this was helpful.
[28:14] [Meeting wraps quickly with brief goodbyes]

Post-call notes (auto-generated):
- Customer is multi-vendor and seeks a pragmatic parity-first migration with pilot benchmarks.
- Priority concerns: latency at spikes, function-call schema parity, and network/VPC constraints.
- Redwood's Optimize product will be used to recommend quantization and batching settings.

Potential risks flagged:
- Tokenization-induced cost deltas may be significant for certain prompt families and need manual prompt engineering.
- Procurement timeline may push Private deployment start date out.

Files to attach (to be sent): parity_mapping_template.xlsx, redwood-soc2-cert.pdf, vpc-requirements.md, pilot-bench-guidelines.docx

End of transcript.
